name: Musaeus
credit: Frederic Leighton, The Last Watch of Hero (c. 1880) · Illustrative image, not a portrait of the poet (none survives) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Musaeus, called Musaeus Grammaticus ("the scholar") to tell him from the legendary singer of the Orphic age, was a Greek poet of about AD 500. He wrote in the school of Nonnus of Panopolis, in polished hexameters crowded with ornate epithets and rhetorical turns. Almost nothing is known of his life.

His one surviving poem is the short epyllion Hero and Leander, some 340 lines in Greek, which tells how a priestess of Aphrodite at Sestos and a youth of Abydos love across the Hellespont, how he swims to her each night by the light of her torch, and how both die when a winter storm puts out the lamp. It is the source of the later English versions, among them George Chapman's of 1616 held here. It is a different poem from Christopher Marlowe's Hero and Leander, which Chapman completed.
